performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The tenors sing their prayer while the violas carry a tune of their own. Fauré lets that string melody have the last word, after the choir has remembered the dark opening of the Requiem.

sections.label: A′ · The tenors return
sections.mNote: The tenor prayer returns over the strings’ independent tune

relations.label: The instrumental melody returns lower
relations.basis: The instrumental close recalls the opening string melody after the Introit quotation, as described in the listening notes. The measured shift is three semitones down, consistent with the opening F-major material returning in D major. CENS diagonal mean 0.912, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift -3 semitones and time offset 320 s (cache/form/faure-requiem-agnus-dei.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: The strings have a tune
cues.text: Violins and violas begin a flowing F major melody. When the tenors enter, they sing a different tune above it. The violas keep going: two melodies share the prayer, with plucked bass notes underneath.
cues.evidence: Fauré, Requiem, Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 70–73: six instrumental bars precede the tenor entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recorded in Monaco
cues.text: Louis Frémaux and the Monte-Carlo orchestra record the Requiem in Monaco in August 1962. The Erato sleeve names the cathedral, Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception, and the date 11 August; Canon Henri Carol plays the organ.
cues.evidence: Erato LDE 3228 sleeve (Internet Archive scan): “Enregistré en la Cathédrale N.-D. de l’Immaculée Conception, à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”; organist Chanoine Henri Carol; direction Louis Frémaux. https://archive.org/details/faure-o-requiem-cantique-de-jean-racine-louis-fremaux

cues.title: The whole choir pleads
cues.text: The other voices join the tenors and the harmony turns towards the minor. Their chords shift uneasily against the viola and cello melody. The strings keep the same walking pace beneath this more urgent appeal.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 74–77: full choral petition over the continuing lower-string melody, with chromatic changes in the choral parts.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The tenor prayer returns
cues.text: The tenors have the prayer to themselves again. F major returns with them, and the violas resume their flowing tune. The other voices rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 77–80: the tenor melody returns with the other choral staves silent.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Light on a held C
cues.text: The sopranos hold C on “Lux” — light. As the other voices gather beneath it, the same note becomes the third of an A♭ major chord. Six choral parts spread out from that single thread of sound.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 80–81: soprano C and the six-part choral entry at rehearsal E, with A♭ in the bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A funeral at the Madeleine
cues.text: Paris, 16 January 1888: Fauré conducts the first version of the Requiem at the Madeleine, for the funeral of the architect Joseph Lesoufaché. There are five movements. The Offertoire and Libera me join the work later.
cues.evidence: Première and revision history, with references to Jean-Michel Nectoux and Jessica Duchen: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

cues.title: Between two bereavements
cues.text: Fauré’s elder son Philippe wrote that his father composed the Requiem “between two bereavements”, and that the luceat eis is surely murmured for those who rocked him as a child, whom he would like to rock in the mysterious beyond.
cues.evidence: Philippe Fauré-Frémiet, quoted in French by Louis Aubert in the sleeve note of the Erato recording (Internet Archive scan): “Entre deux deuils … le luceat eis est tout naturellement murmuré en faveur de ceux qui l’ont bercé”. Translation ours. Fauré’s father died in 1885 and his mother on New Year’s Eve 1887: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9)

cues.title: The opening prayer remembered
cues.text: The music stops, then begins again at Molto largo. The choir returns to “Requiem aeternam” in D minor: the opening of the whole work, recalled inside this movement. The flowing string tune is gone; low strings hold beneath the voices.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 87–89: fermatas, Molto largo, and the reprise of the Introit in D minor.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The strings finish the prayer
cues.text: The choir falls silent. The strings bring back their first tune in D major, a minor third below its original F major. F♯ has replaced the F♮ of the remembered Introit; the organ and plucked basses accompany the last phrases.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 90–91: D major, 3/4, returning string melody and pizzicato bass.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: More voices, darker chords
transitions.how: The F major tenor prayer opens into a full choral petition coloured by minor harmony. Violas and cellos continue the moving tune beneath the choir’s changing chords, with bassoons and horns reinforcing the voices. The beat stays steady as the choral parts climb and grow louder.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 74–77: the second Agnus Dei petition and its continuing lower-string accompaniment.

transitions.title: F major and the tenors
transitions.how: The full choir diminishes and rests. Over the organ’s returning tune and a plucked bass, the tenors begin their first melody again in F major. The violas take up the accompaniment beneath them, marked espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 77–78: diminuendo, organ solo, pizzicato bass and tenor reprise.

transitions.title: C becomes the third of A♭
transitions.to: C · A held C opens Lux aeterna
transitions.how: The tenor prayer settles on C major. The sopranos hold its keynote alone on “Lux”; at rehearsal E, A♭ arrives in the bass and turns that C into the third of a new chord. Altos, divided tenors and divided basses fill out the harmony, pianissimo, while the strings begin to move again.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 80–81: C major close, soprano C, and the A♭ major entry at rehearsal E.

transitions.title: A pause before the Introit
transitions.from: C · A held C opens Lux aeterna
transitions.to: D · The Introit returns in D minor
transitions.how: The strings settle over D, and fermatas stop the music. Common time and Molto largo replace the flowing triple metre. A forceful D fades under the choir’s pianissimo “Requiem aeternam”, restoring the D minor harmony and slow tread of the Introit.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), p. 87: fermatas, change from 3/4 to common time, and Molto largo at the Introit reprise.

transitions.title: D minor opens into D major
transitions.from: D · The Introit returns in D minor
transitions.to: A″ · Strings alone in D major
transitions.how: F♯ brightens the choir’s final chord into D major. The score restores triple metre and the opening pace, and violins and violas recover their flowing melody over a plucked bass. The choir rests for the remainder of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 90–91: the change to two sharps and 3/4, I° Tempo, and the instrumental conclusion.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: V. Agnus Dei, printed pp. 70–91: six bars of strings and organ before the tenor entry, Lux aeterna, the Introit’s return and the D major string coda.

timeline.note: Violins and violas sing above divided cellos, plucked double basses and organ.
The tenors begin “Agnus Dei”; the violas continue their own tune beside them.
Bassoons and horns join the whole choir. Violas and cellos carry the string melody below.
The winds fall silent as the tenors return with strings and organ.
The sopranos hold C. The other voices enter beneath it in A♭ major, with strings, bassoons, horns and organ.
The choir recalls the Introit in D minor, with bassoons, horns, strings and organ.
The choir’s D major chord gives way to the opening string melody.
Strings and organ have the last word in D major. The choir is silent.

composer.epithet: He spent his days at the organ and in the classroom, saving for songs and chamber music the harmonies nobody else could quite imagine.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
The boy kept slipping into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and the little instrument in its chapel gave Gabriel Fauré his first musical happiness. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he lived among plainchant, organ exercises and the interweaving voices of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was done, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers far outside their syllabus. Fauré acquired a teacher, a champion and a friend who would stay beside him for sixty years. He left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine: a French prayer unfolding over a flowing keyboard part, each new choral entry joining a phrase already under way.
